text:
Vista SP2 >>> 7. Especially in the looks department. 7 took Aero and overused it so much it ran it into the ground. Vista's taskbar was perfect. It also introduced nothing major compared to what Vista introduced over XP, so much so that I began calling 7 a 'half assed service pack' to Vista SP2.

Features nobody really used properly? So, UAC which was important to mitigate privilege escalation exploits, is a feature nobody really used? Sure, there's the idiots who turn off UAC, but they shouldn't own devices in the first place. The new driver model admittedly wasn't used at the start which caused Vista's infamous incompatibilities, but by SP2 it's been amazing, and now that driver model is used as the base for all drivers.

Turing was the Windows ME of graphics cards, not Vista. The personal loathing I have for 7 comes from 6 months of absolute headaches it produced me after I switched from Vista SP2 which by the way, handled my Celeron crapbox much better than 7 ever did.

I'm beginning to think the LTT fanbase care more about the entertainment of Linus being a goofy ass out of touch CEO, instead of the technicalities and actually knowing something about tech.

text: Why I bought the EVGA 2080 Super Ftw3. It wasn't for the RTX capabilities, it was for the superior Cooling and 1440p g-sync gaming experience. I don't think the majority of gamers who play first-person or fast action games are concentrating on shading and lighting. I'm sure everybody is familiar with the phrase Tunnel Vision. Let me give you an example. If you're walking down the street your eyes will process a lot more information and you will notice lighting shadows and colors a lot more. If you're driving a car at 50-Mph you're not paying attention to shadows and lighting. All your concentrating is focused on what's appearing in front of you, and your field of view becomes very narrow. Great video, thanks for being honest.

text:
Whoaaaaa, been watching LINUS (not religiously but regularly-ish) since 2015 when I decided to move from CONSOLES TO PC......... When Linus says "SHIT" without a smile on his face being displayed as he says it... AND HE BLEEPS IT... He is fucking serious lmao. My dude Linus looks so disappointed like I've never seen him wtf. I'm surprised I never bothered watching this video when it first came out, I guess I just didn't want to hear the truth but now that I discovered the truth BEFORE hitting play on this video... I was ready for the news to be broken by Linus all these months later about RTX. RTX definitely was not ready at all but I believe NVIDIA did it to make a statement... to AMD... To everyone, and to just simply PUSH the Technology out there. They just wanted to say "HEY! Devs, Consumers, this exists and it's offered by us only (right now) so start looking at this because it's the future of Gaming."


The 2018 launch of RTX was just like the 2016 launch of the HTC VIVE. New technology for a crazy premium price that provides a less than adequate experience that ends up not being so enjoyable (to most) for what they paid. The way I see everyone bashing RTX is the same way I used to see everyone bashing HTC for the VIVE. (me included) It is a rocky and treacherous road for everyone when NEW Technology comes out to the masses. Think about it, this new technology was/is taking it's first ever "baby steps" into the world so what did we REALLY expect?! Have we lost sight of reality? Here's what I think. I think the MASSES haven't been seeing new technology like this being released in so long... That it absolutely SHOCKS them when something so fresh finally does come out. I don't know whether that's a good thing or a bad thing yet. (the fact that we're so slow at bringing out new affordable, but high priced tech for the average consumer it seems) 


Here is another thing I think. I think NVIDIA was a little careless and should've taken more time to hype up RTX and release more info on it more slowly over time until release of it BUT, overall I don't believe they've truly fucked up like so many choose to believe. When the equivalent of the RTX 2080 TI is out in the "wild" somewhere between the year 2020 and 2025 and it costs $699 instead of $1,299 at release. I think it will all have paid off and when new tech that's never really been seen before comes out, and it has a high price tag but is just inside of the realm of affordable for a majority of consumer... *(like with the HTC VIVE and the 2018 launch of RTX GPU's) History will repeat itself, cause that's what history does.

The way I see everyone bashing RTX is the same way I used to see everyone bashing HTC for the VIVE. (me included) It is a rocky and treacherous road for everyone when NEW Technology comes out to the masses. Think about it, this new technology was/is taking it's first ever "baby steps" into the world so what did we REALLY expect?! Have we lost sight of reality? Here's what I think. I think the MASSES haven't been seeing new technology like this being released in so long... That it absolutely SHOCKS them when something so fresh finally does come out for them to take advantage of. I don't know whether that's a good thing or a bad thing yet. (the fact that we're so slow at bringing out new affordable, but high priced tech for the average consumer it seems) 


NVIDIA was a little careless and should've taken more time to hype up RTX and release more info on the tech slowly over time until its release BUT, overall I don't believe NVIDIA have truly fucked up like so many choose to believe. Just watch, when the equivalent of the RTX 2080 TI is out in the "wild" somewhere between the years 2020 and 2025 and it costs $699 instead of $1,299 at release. I think it will all have paid off, and when new tech that's never really been seen before comes out again and it has a high price tag but is just inside of the realm of affordable for a majority of consumers... History will repeat itself, cause that's what history does. Just the fact that new tech will come out again in similar fashion is history repeating itself.

text:
Used and refurbished non-super 20xx series cards might be worth it now, I was able to snag a refurb 2080 for just over £500 which is around the same price as the slightly slower 2070 super and not much more than a used 1080ti.

I say "might" cause AMDs RX 5700 xt is a more than suitable (and cheaper) alternative. At the same time there are games in development that will utilize global Dxr and more current titles are looking to adopt some form of ray tracing so it really comes down to whether you think the technology is worth paying a premium for.

The 2080ti only becomes worth it if you consistently game at 4k as any resolution lower than that can be easily handled by a 2080, 2070 super or even a 1080ti which are ballparks cheaper. Even used it still goes for around £900.

Also depends what you're upgrading from. If you have a 1080ti or even a 1080 non-ti then I would wait for the next generation of cards. If you have a less powerful card then see what kind of performance increases you can get and decide whether or not the amount you would pay seems reasonable. 

TL;DR Used 20 series non-super cards not a bad choice if upgrading from a 1070 and below but the RX 5700 xt is also worth considering. Not really worth upgrading from a 1080 and certainly not worth upgrading from a 1080ti, wait a generation. Only consider a 2080ti if you game at 4k and want the larger memory buffer. The 2060 super should do for anyone who games at 1080p for a good time to come

text:
I believe ray tracing is here to stay. 

Ray tracing really is the next big step in gaming/graphic computation. We've already reached the threshold for acceptable high resolution textures and polygons. Unless you zoom into the smallest detail in a game you will not find any boxy objects or low resolution textures. We've even delt with anti aliasing as we now have many solutions to those disgusting jaggys. To be honest we pretty much reached the threshold back in 2007 with the orginal crysis. Theres a reason why that game still looks great today. Simply by adding lighting mods to crysis the game looks almost as good as games today. Another example would be the battlefield series in the last 14 or so years. Battlefield V objectively looks better than Battfield 3(2011) which is a 7 year older. However, was the leap in grapchis greater with battlefield 2(2005) to battlefield 3 or BF3 to BFV? I think we can all agree battlefield 3 having the greater graphical leap.

We seem to have our focus pushing for higher resolutions which isn't necessary a bad thing but for our games. But this will only help with noticing higher resolution textures from a distance. To unlock CGI level graphics our focus must be on lighting.

text:
I just bought a vega 64 for my new rig. I thought about getting the rtx. I decided it was not worth it at this time, more options will be available for ray tracing by the time software with that feature becomes available. besides that, to your price- I shopped newegg. I got my asus rog strix vega 64 for a price that dipped well into the 4's. Then, I got an "e card" from AMD giving me the new Assasin's Creed game for free, plus two other new release games of my choice(short list available) so basically $150 of free games. Obviously, a flash sale is not standard pricing. But a little shopping around mostly debunks any ideas of "the old cards cost as much as new ones", be it a 1080 vs a 1080ti, Vega card vs a 1080ti, etc. 

There really is little point in buying the new RTX cards unless you actually, for some very niche reason, need the extra GPU power. Buying it to future proof is rather silly, no one knows what that future actually is it is akin to buying a lottery ticket whether or not the extra money now will be worth it. That scenario played out several times with Intels CPU chip sets, with GPU's in the past, etc. Tech gets older, it goes down in price, as a general rule- so waiting until you need the tech to purchase it is a simple way to hedge the bet so to speak. Whats the worst that can happen? It costs the same in 8 months when some game you want comes out with the new tech? Sell the old for a little less, buy the new for a little less, enjoy the current gen's goodies while waiting. 
That's how I looked at it anyway. I picked up one of the "recent best" GPU's on the market for 1/2 to 1/3(depending on model) of the new RTX. Maybe I will decide to buy an RTX next summer. Maybe AMD will release a competitor. Maybe ray trace won't be in the market in any amount worth mentioning until 2020. This is the first time in recent memory where the hardware is trying to sell itself on features no one expects to go mainstream for a long time. The only other item similar I can think of off the top of my head is Physx, and even that is likely to have ended up having a faster roll out then this ray tracing will. 

Thats my take anyway. IMO Nvidea is just trying to cash in on the big kahuna wave from the mining price spike, and they get to set a precedent in release price to boot. It's all win, and all predatory business practices, for Nvidea this time. That also weighed in on my decision.

text:
Furthermore, the main feature is just a card-locked function in game libraries that nVidia is pressuring devs to use.

The algorithm can actually run on ANY card with compute capability, and that EXACT code can run on ANY card with CUDA capability.  

It's literally only locked to the RTX cards to force you to buy a new video card.  No doubt it's performance would be crap on an older card, but that is not to say it wouldn't run.

Still, the performance difference is night and day, which is downright amazing.  If they had focused on this alone, they'd be selling these out without the RTX technology.

Furthermore, the better heterogeneous task core behavior allocation that helps get the most of the RTX code no doubt has other usages in compute tasks that require multiple pipeline types.   This same technology is probably what is part of all these other major performance improvements, as much as the increased raw core count and increased memory bandwidth.

The big thing is, though will be seen on the release of the workstation versions.  Namely, can they beat AMD on memory bandwidth and quantity as well as power-efficiency.  These three sections have been where AMD has been dominating since Vega. 

It will also be interesting to see what new cards AMD plans to release. It's known that a new generation is coming from little bits added to various open source drivers to support them.  However, this only discloses limited information and doesn't including information like the actual specs of the cards.

There's another way to understand this RTX launch:   It's a technical demonstrator for developers and reporters, as it was the original 3DFX Voodoo twenty years ago, and by the time the developers realise and learn how to use the full potential of RTX and DLSS technologies,  the second generation is out, with polished architecture and better design (as it was the Voodoo 2). Actually, they are "Applefinding" the market: launching an unpolished 1st gen of something just to create knowledge and "needing feel in the market" and  dominate  it with 2nd+ generations.

So now we can understand the "new prices" and the stagnation with the 10 series prices: Nvidia presumably wants to create a "value" mental anchor for this new cards, so when the 21 or 30 series are presented in 2020 (to make an educated guess), then they can be presented "for the same price" the 20 series had at launch, with x2 -> x3 performance increase and all the eye candy enabled at day one.
And moreover, now it's the best time to do this hat-trick:  just while being the king on the hill, because AMD's Vega is just not fit to compete with the 10 series, Navi is only a promise and Intel Graphics is cozy in its low power market.

text: I'm not sure why everyone is acting so surprised by this - Leaps forward in Hardware have typically always, and will typically always emerge before the software exists that can fully utilize them. It's not rocket science, nor capitalism taken too far: It's just common sense. How long were HyperThreading CPU's available before the consumer software market finally supported it across the board? And when first released, how expensive were they compared to the previous generation?  Did we have games on CD before CDRom drives were commonly available? Did every game support Adlib sound when that hardware first hit market? Consider being less upset that you can't play realtime raytraced games on a $300 card today, and appreciate that these brand-spanking new technologies will allow you to do so in the future.

text:
Here's the thing with pre-orders of games - you're not committing to buy them at all, just reserving them and getting the pre-order or launch bonus content for doing so (if you actually complete the transaction).  You can ALWAYS cancel it or at the very least, move your pre-order reserve $$ to another game (but I think, legally in the US, the store has to refund you for cancelling a pre-order anyway - if that's not the case tho, I haven't found a store yet that doesn't allow you to cancel them or move your pre-order money to another title).  And I often do, if there is any reason I'm not SURE I want the game, I just cancel my pre-order - no harm done!  Therefore, it's only logical to pre-order, as there is no downside aside from that which comes from the fact that pre-ordering exists at all (like the existence of pre-order bonuses, which I can say aren't often that great but yet I'm always afraid I'll really want them if I don't end up getting them, which has also happened!).  So, pre-ordering is likely here to stay - but it's not that bad anymore, most of the time. 

For hardware, though, it's a bit different.  However, the one bonus to pre-ordering launch cards from a new NVIDIA release, though, is that you can often instantly re-sell them for more money - sometimes a lot more money.  I've literally funded a $650-$800 card more than once just by buying a few of them at launch and selling the extras on ebay immediately, using "in-stock alerts" from whatever service you prefer.

text:
For anyone who has a 1080/1080 Ti now, it's a no brainer: there's no need to upgrade now. However all of these people who think that saving $100-200 on a 1080 Ti purchase compared to the RTX 2080 will pay off in the long run... that's so short-sighted. Unless you're one of those crazy people who upgrade once every 12-18 months, most people who buy a 1080 Ti now will want to keep it at least until late 2020, and many people probably much longer. By then, most AAA games will support Turing-specific features like DLSS/mesh shading/adaptive rendering that will allow the RTX 2080 to blow 1080 Ti's performance out of the water even in conventional rasterized graphics, making it much more future-proof than the 1080 Ti, despite their equal performance with legacy games.
Unless you can find it at fire-sale prices, buying a 1080 Ti today is simply not a good idea, don't let anyone convince you otherwise. It will be much better to buy an RTX 2080 when you can find it at a decent price, or wait until next year and see if AMD forces Nvidia to lower prices and/or Nvidia releases a Turing refresh at 7 nm.

One thing I don't get is that there's all this talk about live Ray Tracing in games, but not the increased performance numbers in Machine Learning which the Tensor Cores in RTX are all about not just DLSS. But most people expect RTX to be judged in FPS in gaming because that's what people are used to judging graphics cards on. Its hard to benchmark something if the Ray Tracing/Machine Learning because its a new bar set that has nothing to compare itself to, or even have games released to support it, other than cards without the technology.

People forget that new technology RTX is also aimed at realtime rendering for VFX productivity (expecting to benchmark in Blender at launch is laughable) and Machine Learning, and not just video games. So while I agree with Linus on NVIDIA having a very disorganized launch, RTX doing "NOTHING" is a bit of hyperbole.

text:
This scenario isn't that different from when the original Geforce launched with TnL (Hardware Transform and Lighting) in 1999.  It ended up being a revolutionary feature (one of the main reasons graphics saw such an incredible surge in polygon counts in the early to mid 2000s), but at launch it was supported by virtually no games.  At launch, there was probably less application support for TnL than for RTX.  

Yet, the fact that Nvidia were the first to push Hardware Transform and Lighting to market, even with few applications that supported it at release, ended up being a huge win for them.  Ultimately, it played a role in their victory over 3dfx, who were planning to include Hardware TnL in a later generation when more games would support it.  Needless to say, it didn't work out well for them.  

Historically, there's something to be said for pushing features and getting a product out the door rather than letting feature-creep delay a product (a contributor to the downfall of 3dfx).  And honestly, compared to TnL, RTX has pretty stellar application support.  Pushing features ahead of their competitor's product cycles is how Nvidia has come to dominate the market.  And honestly, waiting weeks to months instead of years to see a whole host of RTX supported games is actually pretty good when you take a look back.

text: Blender's getting some larger updates in the near future, and support is growing, which means it's going to be a viable option to use when working alone or in small groups. It doesn't have support for large production pipelines, but it is a solid tool for enthusiasts. In regards to GPU usage, you're much better using Redshift or Octane for Maya and C4D instead, if you want to leverage realtime ray tracing. GPU's only factor into 3D program work view spaces, not rendering, so benchmarks for high end GPU's will mostly look the same from card to card. GPU rendering is the future, and it's what the RTX was designed for. The potential is higher than what the common perception has been. Real time ray tracing is a HUGE deal, but until the feature is adopted, the cards wont be utilized to their potential. It's like trying to use a calculator to solve a problem without batteries.

text: Thomas  If we look at current AA rendering techniques, such as supersampling, you can play at 1080p while simulating a higher resolution. The point that I'm making is the jump from 1080p to 3K and 4K, and then from 4K to 8K is just not noticeable enough to warrant the price spikes. author: @gorehound666

text:
Supersampling doesn't do what you think it does, it doesn't "simulate a higher resolution". Your GPU processes each frame as though it were a higher resolution and then scales it back down to a 1080p image. This can produce a better looking 1080p image, but it's still a 1080p image. Obviously you're still going to be physically limited by the number of pixels on the display, ie there is a hard cap on how detailed the image can ever get. If you think super sampling a 1440p or 4k image on a 1080p display is anything like an actual 1440p/4k display, you're very mistaken.

On a large monitor that your face is 1-2 feet away from, going above 1080p absolutely does make a difference. Clearly you need to see it for yourself. Moving from a large 1080p monitor to a 27" 1440p was probably the biggest upgrade I've ever made. There's a reason monitors like the ROG Swift have been so popular.

text:
I'm with ya man. From a gamer's perspective, this whole release looks like a pile of promises and not much delivery.  It is very disappointing.  But I understand WHY it is like this.  The whole theory behind RTX is changing the way games are programmed, so this is gonna require a HUGE change in the way game studios work.  This is not going to be a big change with the card, this is going to be a gradual change in the games that come out.  This whole gamble by nVidia is about taking a bet that people will adopt this in the future.  It's risky on their end, but as you said, with their track record, it will likely pay off.  But not immediately.

That being said, those of us who are using these cards for workstations, we are smiling ear to ear.  The company Otoy, makers of Octane Render (who's results can be seen in the Westworld intro) has been optimizing their render engine to use RTX.  At the moment, they HAVEN'T gotten Vulkan in the mix (that they are working on next year) and they are ALREADY reporting 6-8x speed increases over Pascal cards.  So these cards, once the software starts fully supporting it, will be BEASTS for anyone looking to do anything 3D related.  And for me, that's EXACTLY why I want them.

text:
Insane price aside Turing is probably the most significant
performance increse compared with previous generation, but the problem is, unlike previous generations it's true potential must me utilised first in order to show it. Currently results can vary from 25% to 68%, and even the same game can show big differences in the same location. In the most demanding lication in wolfenstein 2 new 2080ti totally kills 1080ti.  50fps min and 61 fps average on 1080ti while new 2080ti runs 90fps min and 90fps and 103 average (111fpa woth OC), that's around 68% increase. There are also other games like hellblade or tomb raider where I can see very big differences in demanding locations. Most games that run at 40-45 fps now runs at 60fps on 2080ti, and any gamer should tell difference. So 2080ti even in current games can be up to 68% faster compared to 1080ti, in the near future when games will start using Turing features that performance difference will be even bigger. Additional 20% thanks to new shading features, 20% more in HDR games, 70-100% more with DLSS, and few months from now leople will see results around 150% better compared to pascal. Turing price is insane but if someone has money and want the best 4K experience, then 2080ti is the only card that can provide 60fps in most games.

text:
When it comes to raytracing in games... duh?  A card has to be first to the market with that kind of capability for developers and their multi-year cycles for game development to be able to sit down and code things for it, maybe incorporate it into an entire engine rather than just patch it in, really learn it and get good with it, etc.  We would never get anywhere in tech if we waited for 20 games to support a piece of technology before any hardware for said technology comes out.

I said this about Vulkan years ago being a game changer when it was brand new and I said it was going to be years off before Vulkan had any hope at all of turning some heads because again, people have to actually incorporate it into their dev cycles.  It's been 2 and a half years since the first Vulkan-supported game hit the scene and the list of games that support Vulkan is still paltry.

I think the message is don't buy this thing for raytracing because practically nothing supports it, and by the time you'll start getting handfuls of games using it, the NEXT generation of cards would be viable to grab if you really want raytracing.  For me, I'd be interested in getting a performance boost this generation.  I have a GTX 980, so I'd be interested in either the 2080 series or the 2070 series just from a performance standpoint.

text:
This release by Nvidia is definitely different than anything I've seen since I started PC gaming. It's been clear for a while before now that the traditional performance of these cards is basically equivalent to their existing products. For first time PC builders who want a high-end rig or people that were planning on upgrading their GPU around this time (which includes me), the situation is decent: once the prices reach MSRP for the 2080 (and this applies to the 2070 but not the 2080 Ti since it has no equivalent), I can get a brand new GPU with some very cool tech and somewhat better performance than last gen, with that gap improving over time. There's a moderate price premium ($500 for an RTX 2070 vs. $450 for a new GTX 1080) for this but it's not a bad deal with all factors under consideration.

For people who already have a high-end gaming rig that want bleeding-edge technology and best-of-the-best performance, well, Linus really explains better than I could. You're abusing your wallet very harshly and that bleeding edge tech really isn't doing anything right now. 

From a balanced perspective, it's disappointing, I guess, considering the leaps that new Geforce generations have made before. But we all know why this is happening. AMD's product line has failed to keep up with Nvidia in the realm of high-end gaming performance, and Nvidia has massively higher market share across every tier of GPU performance. For the time being Nvidia has a lot of freedom. They aren't necessarily ripping off the consumer since these aren't worse products, but they are certainly going to increase their margins by shifting their price tiers upwards.

author: @refract8491

text:
Can't be. If people can't buy Ray tracing cards, then companies won't develop for ray tracing, and if no one develops for ray tracing, then no one will buy it, and if no one buys it, then no one will develop for it. So it's a dead technology on arrival. The marketing point of the RTX cards is ray-tracing. There's no real reason to buy them outside of that, but no one is going to support it, especially when consoles won't be able to run it. This means rasterization is still gonna need to be used, which means ray-tracing is extra development time on products, which means larger investment costs for less returns.

RTX stands to make MORE MONEY if we bring out a way to give people an easy in to adopting the technology. We already know that mobile gpus, when dedicated to ray tracing can pull the same ray tracing performance as a RTX 2070. Allowing ray tracing to be offloaded to a secondary gpu would allow console developers to include low power, cheap secondary mobile gpus in their consoles to support ray tracing, which in turn would boost the adoption rate of ray tracing and thus the adoption rate of RTX...

text: PBR shaders accomplish essentially the same effect of ray tracing.  Difference being PBR is locked to a preset environment image. but engines like Unreal are able to basically capture HDR images on the fly which can constantly update the PBR env image.  Real time ray tracing is cool but PBR (physically based rendering) workflows have been around for years and are quite simple to setup and not over taxing on GPUs.  Real time ray tracing may be the future.. im not sold yet.

text:
I have a theory on why Nvidia pulled the launch of the RTX cards before any game availability.

There is a chicken and egg problem, it is hard to convince studios to take ray tracing into use if there are no consumers who would use it, also it does not make sense as a consumer to purchase the product if there are no games that support the feature. 

This is all well and fine, however what makes this all interesting is that Nvidia is working on studios to add the support, they could have delayed the release until there is something out there to test and only launch then. Why they did not do this?

The only plausible thing i can think of for creating this hype and pre-order-mania is as follows: The performance is not there yet. If Nvidia would have launched the cards with the games, the reviewers would have tested them and if the performance impact is big enough, would have discouraged people from buying stuff. 

Now with this pre-order hype Nvidia has managed to push some cards on a promise, that will then help them to push the feature to the studios: "look there are already consumers willing to pay for games with RTX support out there." If this is the case then it really sucks. The correct way of going about this would be to have either the performance or the price point attractive enough for the consumers to buy the cards regardless of the ray-tracing features, which would then make it easier sell for the studios, even with slightly lower profit margins. Now they are trying to have their cake and eat it at the same time. We all know how well that usually works.

nVidia crammed 4352 CUDA cores + 576 Tensor cores + 72 RT cores + geometry units / texture units / ROP units / blah blah blah.
You're all basing the "performance gain" from the GTX 1080ti on rasterization alone.

Great review! Pretty much what I've been thinking. I'm sticking with my 1080. I'm still on a 1920x1080 display here. I have no need for an RTX series card unless I decide to get a 4K monitor. Hell I don't even need a 1080 for 1920x1080 so I'm pretty well set for the long run. At this point I'd only get one if I were a few generations behind on my graphics card and looking to do a massive upgrade and even then, it's a tough sell for those high prices.

I feel like this is the result of nVidia being on top for so long. AMD really needs to help us all out and come up with something that'll compete with nVidia on the high end cards so we can see prices get driven down. Also looking forward to seeing what Intel does with their graphics cards, but I'm not getting my hopes up yet for team blue. In the meantime, yeah, this is the shit that gives PC gaming a bad rap. This is when consoles get more popular and PC gamers stop buying the latest cards for a while forcing game devs to hold back on the amount of resources they can pump into the new tech since they have to still support the older tech. I certainly won't buy a new game if it relies too heavily on features exclusive to hardware I do not have access to. The game will need to support and run great on what I have now. Otherwise I'll be buying the game long after price drops when I finally can afford to do a hardware refresh (If I buy the game at all at that time).

Ray tracing isn't superior in every way, a rasterized image with all the wizardry game developers use to make the image look good can end up looking better than just using raytracing and letting things simulate "realistically". And it being more realistic doesn't make it better looking.
Also raytracing as of now its just approximate raytracing with denoising, so in the end its just different ways of approximating a good looking image, because when making the game they are also approximating it (plus the artistic touch the developer wants to add).

And in the end i prefer a less accurate / realistic image that looks good, than a more realistic image that is noisier / blurrier.

Ill say this again, "Real Time Ray Tracing" is a gamble feature or gimmick. Theres been tons of them through time. 3dTVs, HD DVD, Beta Max, Curved TVs, etc. People spent big money banking on those products being the beginning of the focal point of future technology, and they're getting the honor of being near the forefront of it all.

However, it was just that: a gamble. Find me a soul on this planet that will say "Well yeah but can it run with Ray Tracing on high?" Ray Tracing is NOT the end-all-be-all graphics setting in the history of graphics settings, and its hard to think its worth spending an extra $400 on a GPU thats ALREADY $800 for the benefit of that technology.

DLSS is obviously something specific to nvidia, you couldn't just port that across to AMD(even if AMD added hardware to support Deep Learning), this is why nvidia is doing the deep learning for free to developers.

Hybrid raytracing is the future for gaming graphics. It is just a matter of when, not if.

author: @DrFMA

text:
Intel's prices are down to poor strategy, stagnant tech, and much higher cost. Their chips cost so much more to produce that they have to charge more than AMD. Intel's really in a bad place with the Core architecture at the moment because the price per CPU rises almost exponentially as they add cores due to their monolithic chip design. AMD's design is nearly as fast, wildly flexible, and FAR less expensive to produce. If Zen 2 has the IPC and frequency improvements it's rumoured to have, they'll really have Intel over a barrel, since Intel will lose its single-core IPC advantage, which is all it has right now. 
GPU-wise, it's almost the opposite. Vega is huge, expensive, and slow. AMD doesn't have the cash to field multiple SKUs per generation the way Nvidia does, so they can't target specific tasks and segments the way Nvidia can. Vega is Ryzen in reverse. Ryzen is tiny, easy-to-produce chips ganged up to cheaply scale to any task they need to. Vega is a jack-of-all-trades GPU using exotic memory, and gets beaten by more specifically targeted Nvidia hardware in nearly every class it competes in, while being too expensive to scale down effectively. AMD needs to find a way to sucker-punch Nvidia the way they did Intel, but Nvidia's a more agile company, and definitely sees AMD coming for them. That's why I think 2020 is make or break for RTG. They'll have time (and money, finally) to come up with a "GPU Ryzen," likely using chiplets or MCM, but Nvidia's also researching MCM tech, and Koduri probably picked a few things up before he went to Intel. 2020 will be vicious, but Nvidia owns 2018 and 2019, no contest.

text:
+nighterlev 
I'd like to know where you're getting this from, since all the info I've heard indicates that Navi will be a Polaris replacement, i.e. a midrange card to scrap with the 2060 and below. Navi will probably be a really great option for the majority of people who don't want to spend more than 300 bucks on a GPU, but it will top out where Polaris does in the stack. 
The Xbox One X GPU, by the way, is not a 1070, it's an AMD custom part based on Polaris that is closest to an RX480 in performance, so definitely not GTX 1070-level performance. The 1070 has an estimated 45% performance lead over it. 
Nvidia may not release a new architecture until 2020, but they will more than likely have a refresh for next year once Nvidia can get their mitts on 7nm. It's no secret that RTX, even on the 2080Ti, performs pretty poorly, but with a die shrink and the performance bump that comes from that, they can MAYBE hit 60 FPS at 1080p with RTX on, which might be good enough for some folks. They can have that ready for next year no problem, and they know people will buy it, so why not?
I think the RTX launch is hugely flawed, don't get me wrong. They're too slow at their headline feature on current software, let alone the stuff that will be out by the time RTX is adopted enough to be at all relevant, and the performance uplift in normal games is terrible considering how much they cost. These are bad cards now, they'll age horrendously and nobody should buy them for gaming, they should get a 1080Ti instead. However, at 35% higher than the 1080Ti's already impressive gaming performance, I highly doubt AMD has an answer to the 2080Ti at the ultra high-end.
I don't think that AMD has some kind of silver bullet up their sleeve. I think they're working on it, and like I said, they've assembled just the guys to do it and they finally have some cash in their pockets. David Wang was part of the SGI/ArtX team that developed the Flipper GPU for Nintendo's GameCube, which would get beefed up into the legendary Radeon R300 series, and he worked on the HD4000 series, so he's got a great pedigree of making small, fast chips, which is exactly what they need now that GCN has kind of spun out of control.
I'd love for AMD to give Nvidia the kind of bloody nose they gave Intel, but I think you're expecting WAY too much out of Navi.

And no one can make you change your mind about how nvidia is cool because in the end...the product is and will be good. This approach can look "rushed" and "weird" from nvidia. RX580 $329.99 Newegg

Take Overwatch for example.
Gtx 1080, 1080p ultra, 300+fps. (game caps out at 300.)  4k Ultra. 110fps- 130 fps.
Rx580  1080p ultra, 90-140 fps. 4k Ultra, 25-30 fps.

Also V-Sync in games has an input lag of <1 millisecond. 
Last game I experienced tearing in was skyrim, ( and thats for an entirely different reason.)

Now. I cant advocate the new cards. They use useless technology with space and cost that could have gave us more cuda cores for a much better performance margin.

Adeptus Astartes Ehh, neither of those things are true though. 1440p/144Hz monitors have been really popular for several years now. Ever heard of the ROG Swift? I would guess very few people who are spending money on high end GPU's are wasting the performance on 1080p gaming. Go look at completed builds on pcpartpicker etc, and you'll see that most high end builds are using a 1440p/144Hz monitor. I've personally been using one with a 1080 for a couple years now, and there are definitely games like Battlefield 1 where I'm only getting 75-100 fps with max-ish settings at 1440p (so presumably a 1080ti isn't going to be getting 144 either). 

Also, that a game would be "optimized" for 1080p but not for 1440p is not a real thing lol, since all it is is scaling up the resolution. 1440p is a bit less than twice as many pixels as 1080p - if you look at benchmarks you'll see that the fps difference between the two is usually at around that ratio.
author: @4lc441

text:
Adeptus Astartes I've been using a 1440p/144Hz monitor for several years now and have never run into any resolution related problem, and play or have played several of the games you mentioned. Maybe there was a point where games were having issues at higher resolutions, but that certainly hasn't been the case for the last several years.

1440p/144hz/gysnc displays are really expensive, but so are the GPU's you need to take advantage of them - it's the same people buying both. You'd be dumb to spend $800+ on a GPU and use it at 1080p, when something like a 1060 will max out most games anyway. The only reason to spend that much on a GPU is to take advantage of higher resolution/refresh rate monitors. Right now 1440p/144Hz is the sweet spot for high end GPU's.

Edit: Also, a server can't lock the refresh rate of your monitor lol. The server tick rate has 0 impact on your fps or refresh rate. If your gpu is spitting out 144 fps, and your monitor is refreshing 144 times per second, you're going to see 144 fps regardless of whatever the server is doing.

text:
I'm not an "early adopter." I don't want to defend the position of the "early adopter."

I certainly don't want to defend that Tom's hardware article. 

Given this video, it seems to me that these new 20 series cards are good cards. Based off of Linus' numbers (and all the other benchmarks that I've seen), the 2080ti is the best possible card that you can get (excluding something like the titan V, but are we really going to bring a $3k card into this?). Therefore, its value is relative to how much you care about having the best possible hardware. Asking what the "value" of a 2080ti is like asking what the value of a Ferrari is. The 2080ti really is, no joke,  equivalent (give or take) to a 3000 dollar card. No one looks at the Titan V and says "that's not worth it" because you don't get a card like that to play overwatch, but now you potentially can.

Is the 2080 a better buy than the 1080ti? Ehhhhhh probably not for your average gamer.

But don't forget that these cards do have tensor cores, and graphics cards today have lots of other applications other than just playing crysis. If you participate in any open source deep learning projects, I think it would actually be worth the extra 150 to 200 bucks to get a 2080 of a 1080ti. But again, that's not your average gamer. And, on that note, I wonder how much of this DLSS, and tensor core junk is really just a consequence of AI and deep learning development. Don't forget that Nvidia spends an assload of money on development for this, and it only makes sense that they'd try and find a way to incorporate it into mainstream consumer hardware. While it might not make complete sense right now, maybe it will in the future. But that's just the problem: Nvidia should just be honest about that and explain that this is an experiment. I don't understand why they can't just be transparent about that, because its obvious that's what this is.

But I do want to end saying that for the most part I agree with you. There's way too much hype about these 20 series cards, and it really is foolish to preorder anything. I just see people end up falling on the other side of the spectrum who weren't waiting for the benchmarks either. But now that they're here we can just look. The verdict is in. These are not budget cards; however, if you want the best possible gaming experience, we can now definitely say, with 100% certainty, that the card you want is the 2080ti.

But honestly, who expected these to be "budget" cards? Honestly, who would think that Nvidia would release a new line of products that are cheaper than an older line that they still have a large stock of? If you're considering buying one of these 20 series cards, then you're someone who likes having a lot of computing power (regardless of whether or not you use it). Honestly, what I can't figure out is why Nvidia released the 2080 and the 2080ti at the same time.

The 2080ti makes sense to me, but the 2080 just doesn't.

text:
It is a bit of a misnomer that RTX can do raytracing. It doesn't.
It uses a raycasting raytracing. The theory is that tracing the light starting from the camera is the same as tracing it from each light. It isn't the same, but close enough.
There is also some light fudging to get things to look better. Also only 6 light sources can interact on the same surface in RTX. In general a person can only perceive up to 8 light sources on a surface in real life. As a programmer you currently also have to limit how many surfaces you mark as for use by RTX, because it can't do full scene raycasting raytracing in real time.
After taking all these caveats into account, this will still make things look better, but the hardware is in the early stages and has its limitations. It sounds like the APIs also have their limitations and will probably get iterated upon quickly in the next few years, which may hamper adoption.

The cards are good at rasterization, but that increase in performance alone is not worth the massive increase in price.

Also, I think ray tracing will be a great technology and make games look much better, but I just don't think the performance will be there in the first gen of GPUs. I think most people will opt to turn the features off and play at higher resolutions and frame rates.

text: Is it just me or is it obvious that Nvidia just slid up their traditional naming scheme to justify the massive increase in prices we see compared to each cards relative predecessor. Further the 1070 was above the 980 Ti in perf, as we see here with the 2080 vs the 1080 Ti, meaning the 2080 is essentially a 2070, only now it costs $699 instead of $369. As for the 2070, its perf will be below that of the 1080 Ti,  making it far more appropriately considered as #60 class gpu than a #70 class gpu. text:
To be perfectly fair, there's no way for developers to really build their games on this tech if it doesn't launch.  So 2 more years in the future if we didn't have RTX, there would still be no RTX games because there's no RTX.  The hardware has to come first before it can be utilized.  The prices imo are mostly justified, but the founders edition cards are the problem.  For example, the 2080 should be $700 (on par with the 1080ti) but the cards that people can buy right now are way more than that.  Buying a new 2080 over a 1080ti would give you very similar performance, but with Tensor cores and RT cores built into the card that can be unlocked at a later date.  But nobody is paying that 1080ti price for 1080ti performance because of the stupid overpricing of the initial launch.

Essentially, the MSRP of the new cards mostly match price to performance of the previous generation of cards and they have a promise to add in more, but they're selling above MSRP and that's the biggest problem here.  I could get behind paying 700 bucks for 1080ti performance today because that's what the cost of it was for the last 2 years (not counting the prices during the mining craze), but only if the new cards actually had more going for them.  The fact we're paying more for the same performance when it reaches us, the comsumers, is what's going to really kill this card.  The only positive thing here is that the hardware exists now for the development to go through for games, but ultimately, we still lose.

text:
This situation of a powerful, fast new card with a feature set that wasn't used anywhere outside of benchmarks felt familiar, but I couldn't quite put my finger on it until I saw a comment on TechReport; this is the GeForce 3 all over again, over seventeen years ago. At that time the only thing that really supported pixel shaders was 3DMark 2001, and the "must have" game that would use the technology was going to be Doom 3. Which got pushed back to 2004, when a GeForce 4 or a Radeon 9700 Pro stomped all over the GeForce 3's performance. The preliminary number's I've seen with ray-tracing turned on (over at Ars Technica) at 4k or 1080p upsampled to 4k are still below 60 fps even in carefully structured demos like the Star Wars elevator one.

Ray tracing could dramatically revolutionize how we render games once developers and hardware manufacturers get everything coordinated. I just don't know if the RTX 2080 and 2080 Ti are the cards one should buy if they plan on keeping this hardware for four years or so.

text: Ehh... Nvidia needs to focus more on speed rather than ray tracing right now. Ray tracing was never meant for games, it's only used in animation studios where digital 3D animations NEED to look real. Ray tracing in video games, however, is more of a cherry on top than a new game changing feature. I've particularly never had a passion for shadows in games, it's what I care about the least. I always turn it the lowest it can go, and it still looks fine. Honestly, I feel like particle effects and Physx are the future. We need to work on features like this, that could make such a huge difference in gaming. Particle effects are so interesting to play with and can make things so convincing. Physx is the future of huge crumbling skyscrapers in videogames, and actual gas grenades that fill the room with smoke. Oh yeah, did I forget to mention the synthesizing of artificial sound? We can use it to simulate the air vibrations to make the very sound that would come from that object in real life. In real time. No prerecorded sound effects. These would all be truly game changing features. Ray tracing is just not ready yet. We can already make convincing lighting effects that are not at all as resource demanding as this. So, Nvidia, let's try to focus on some other features in the coming years, ok?

text:
Nice video Linus, finally someone who understands Raytracing :) 

Although i must add a few things that you are not taking into consideration and voids your rant at the end.

This isn't rushed, its process that needs to be handled a step at a time from a variety of complex angles. 

You can't get game devs to make games if they don't have the cards. So you can't expect games without the hardware being released first. Especially when it's such a big jump in technology.

Cart before the horse, as they say. 

Also, even though game devs get their hands on the cards in a few weeks, there will also not suddenly be a rush of optimized games for you to run more benchmarks on, as you will see the same results. They need to wait for the game dev engines to do their part first.

Tech like this does not simply just happen at the flick of a switch. It's a long procedure. This is the reason that the game dev company you spoke to had to put things on hold and BF1 is also delayed. 

It's a simple matter of time required to implement all this new tech into their current code architecture software. That's no simple task.

The development software teams such as UE4 and Unity (or in-house software like frostbite etc) need to first code this new architecture into their game engines, BEFORE game devs can make use of it and only THEN implement it into their game titles.  Even though they say Frostbite has RTX, i assure you they haven't had nearly enough time to optimize it and you will see many patches coming in the near future for exactly this.

The other very important factor behind the RTX architecture is the fact that it has 3 cores which when implemented and utilized properly will leave the 1080 in its dust. 

The easiest of those is to implement DLSS, with raytracing being the most difficult. Current games running on TSAA are still putting massive burden off the SM core of the RTX because it's simple not optimized to do anything else. Once done or DLSS is coded into more games and being put onto the Tensor Core where it should be, will you see improved results.

Then there is the matter of drivers. We don't even have DXR yet, so basically all these games are running off rasterization and an unoptimized RT for SotTR.

You also have to consider a point of view for the game development companies, which I can conclude by you thinking that they simply “bailed”, that you don't have very much experience in, on what goes on behind the scenes, when making a game from an artist or coders point of view. 

Making the games you benchmark, look as good as they currently do using rasterization is nothing more than a massive pain in the ass. These artists are insanely talented to achieve what you see with such an old and limited technology. It's temperamental, tedious and takes months of late nights, hacking something together, to try recreate real life lighting, while knowing fully well you'll never achieve it. 

With RT this all becomes MUCH easier, as the computer now does all that heavy lifting for you as an artist, while achieving lighting and texture result that you would never be able to with rasterization. Now you are free to be an artist and not a graphic hacker. 

What does this mean? 

Well less time spent on unnecessary game development, which could either be spent elsewhere. Frame rates are just a small part of what goes into a quality gaming experience. 

If the music in a game is crap, or the AI sucks, the story is bad or networking doesn't work, you hate the game far more than if it runs a few FPS slower. Perfect example is when WOW servers are down during expansion releases. At that point no one cares for frame rates, because with now servers, there are 0 frame to be had. You just don't realize that these other elements exists because they are usually done so well in AAA games. They do however take an enormous amount of time and skills and money to get to this level of excellence, much like the graphical department.

Now with the help of RT and AI these studios or indies, have to put much less effort into their graphics, allowing them to allocate either time or money into making these other elements even better or releasing content faster.. 

Quicker turnover time for their game means more content DLCs/expansions or more time and budget spent on the multitude of other factors that make up a quality game, as mentioned above.

There is more to making a game than just frame rates

As an ex-3d artist and hobbyist indie game dev, i promise that making even the most basic game is no simple task and the reason why so many “fail”. The graphical part with rasterization is a massive time sink, leaving no time or money left to do everything else. RTX now has the potential to be a massive assistance in this. With this many more indies with less budget than AAA studio have a higher chance to finish a really good looking game.

This is why Jensen is so excited. He see the future potential. Do yourself a favor and go onto a 3D artist forum. You won't see a single complaint, as they know the true potential the RTX brings. 
Editing software such as Resolve as also going to be using the AI core in their interface. These cards are more than just about games anymore and as an editor i'm really excited about this and the power it holds for us in the future.

People can benchmark all they want right now, they are really meaningless, other than to tell you that your current 1080ti is still fine for now.

Devs will have to support both rasterization and RT for probably the next year or three, as many people will still want to play their games using a 1080. But once RTX becomes more of a household item, devs with have no love lost for rasterization and will happily never want to see it again, buy which time 1080s will become doorstops.

However, at this point is much better to buy a 1080 ti for current titles, no argument there. But the current benchmarks here will change very quickly over then next 6 to 12 months once most game studios and game engine developers have had time to properly optimized their games and the drivers for RTX. 

This is a summary of my article, where i've written the above as well as more info on each specific tech of the RTX to help more people understand that it's more than just FPS as in the past and that we have to just be patient. 

 https://www.fullexposure.photography/nvidia-turing-rtx-raytracing-explained/ 

Thanks

text:
Yeah, unfortunately, with performance like that in traditionally rendered applications, anyone who wants to play at higher resolutions will probably buy one anyway. Ray tracing when it finally arrives will likely be a little bonus, but not a serious consideration. The main market for the 2080ti is people with 3440x1440 or 3840x2160 monitors who want to maintain 120 or 60 fps respectively in the latest titles on ultra settings. The 1080ti just isn't quite powerful enough, so a 20-30% improvement is more than enough to justify the purchase IMO.

What's worrying now is the huge performance lead that Nvidia has over Radeon cards. The 1080ti already crushed anything coming from the red corner, and the 2080ti is another level higher again. The exorbitant pricing on the 20 series cards is no doubt due to Nvidia's confidence in their rock solid position at the high end of the market. There's simply no alternative. AMD better get their asses in gear before they fall behind any further.

text:
How can you say people are idiots for buying this gpu.
 If your just looking at standard gaming yes the price is very high for the slight performance increase. And I would suggest then people should buy 2 1080ti's sli then. If all you want is a smoother maxed out 4k game. But don't call them idiots. 

 The problem is your only looking at that aspect. This card does have more Cuda cores than a 1080ti and it also has with it rtx and dlss. Which no games use atm (I know).
 But, one key thing your forgetting. If you do 3d rendering (I do btw). The 2080ti beats out the titan V. That's pretty impressive, especially on the price performance on that. So don't say people are idiots for buying a gpu. When all your looking at is gaming with it. Gpu's are used for workstations as well. 
 What people don't realize is if your just gaming. You see the price very high for a 23% improvement. But if you add the tensor cores that can do rtx and dlss. The price is high but isn't that bad. You are paying for that in the card. They aren't going to give that tech away for free.

 When it comes to rendering scenes. People spend a lot of money just to shave off a min of a scene rendering. Cause that time adds up. I have a scene right now 4k hdr. One frame ray tracing is 22hrs render time. Do the math for a 10sec video, 60 frames a sec. It's about 3 months not stop rendering. But I might be able to get the same scene done in 2 months time with a 2080ti. That saves me money on power use alone. And gives me more time. I can start working on something else a month sooner. 

 BTW, I didn't buy this card yet. I probably will get a 2080ti maybe two. But that's for rendering really, gaming would be second for me on this card. So if I did buy this, am I an idiot cause I bought a gpu for $1,200 that beats out in rendering a gpu last year that went for $3,000.

text:
You know, while RT is quite a cool technology and can do lots of cool things, the thing they don't tell you about is what it cannot do.
RT is a physical equivalent of geometrical optics and as such can only realistically calculate within that limit. But one of the most important aspects of light we can also see in our everyday life is scattering. And scattering cannot be calculated within the limit of geometrical optics.
While this potentially could be a huge issue and is the reason why you mostly only see large, smooth objects in RT demos, there are probably ways to account for scattering in RT as well. But that ofc takes more time and thus performance. 
It's a cool solution that works excellent within the geometrical optics limit, but it's not the savior of 3D graphics.

Haha, it actually INCREASED their value because, arguably, a 1080Ti is significantly better than the 2080 (non-Ti), for a lot less money - due to one main reason alone... VRAM.  8GB ALREADY isn't enough for all games at 4K/Ultra settings, like Shadow of War.  11GB is the reasonable MINIMUM that the 2000 series should have started with, otherwise you literally have less VRAM available than the console version of a particular game does (given that they are more efficient with memory use than a PC game can be)... and your performance, or texture quality, suffers as a result.  

The 1080Ti is the best high-end value at this point, especially because usable/desirable RTX features are a long enough way off that there will be another series of cards, maybe more, before we see many games that use RTX well enough to be worth it... and considering the performance cost of the features as they are rumored to be, these cards won't be able to do Ray Tracing at a "good-enough" degree to even really matter, given that the performance cost isn't going to be worth it yet.  WAIT FOR THE NEXT GENERATION!

text: John L - I'd encourage you to think that through a little more, as you're ignoring one KEY thing:  VRAM.  The 1080 Ti has 11GB, the 2080 (non-Ti) has 8GB, and the 1080 Ti can be gotten "near new" (but opened or slightly used) for less than $500 on eBay (~$300 less than you're going to get a decent 2080 card for - which is almost 50% more in cost!).  11GB is the minimum required memory for high-end gaming ALREADY, as games that are already a year old need more than 8GB for their "4K quality" textures running at (or near) 4K resolution (such as Middle Earth: Shadow of War). Since when does "next gen leap" actually happens over night? When NVidia introduced GPU + CUDA it took a while for developers to learn and update all the game engines. CUDA was out for several years before ML researchers realized "hey I can speed up NN with CUDA linear algebra routines". I remember thinking "when will researchers use CUDA for ML?" several years before it happened. Back in 2002 I thought it was time for ML researchers to use FPGA to accelerate ML. I even had lengthy conversations with a friend about it. It wasn't until Microsoft started Brainwave that a general purpose ML -> FPGA framework was created. text:
Kacpa2  This is blatantly false. Reflections and lighting can be implemented in a raster pipeline, but nowhere near the quality of raytraced equivalents. Raster lighting doesn't support hybrid hard/soft shadows (take a long object, and hold it next to a light like *| and look at the difference between the shadow near the floor and the shadow from the top of the pole). Additionally, emissive materials just don't work at all without shitty voxel-based approximations. Reflections are also horrible - screenspace reflections are laughably bad most of the time.

RTX promised something amazing, and if they can get off their asses and make it work, it will be.

text:
Okay look. We grudgingly put up with video games that are at best late beta when they are released, but hardware shouldn't be like software. I shouldn't be made to buy a 2080Ti or whatever and then wait months for a driver patch or for games to 'catch up'

Plus according to the benchmarks, my suspicion was correct: the card's cost to performance ratio means that the only reason to buy is to make use of it at the upper performance. It outperforms the 1080Ti in 4k gaming and likely in rendering. So now video game developers can make use of that, and eventually the 1080Ti will not be able to keep up with newer titles.

but until we see that, buying it now is buying a promise of the future. and I'm not cool with that. All this is teaching me is that if I am due for a gpu upgrade, I should wait a couple of generations and buy the previous generation card. It won't be bleeding / cutting edge but it will save me a bundle

text: Seems like many people don't understand which "PhysX" Robbaz is referring to. Originally it was marketed as a separate processor on an expansion card much like a graphics card, and the main point was hardware acceleration of physics calculations. After NVIDIA acquired it (Ageia PhysX), they put the support for accelerating physics on their cards/gpus and then you could use that to run PhysX supporting games with hardware acceleration (very few games). Meanwhile a generic software physics library/engine also called "PhysX" was developed, which did not REQUIRE the PhysX hardware to run (think Havok, or any other physics engine). This is what "PhysX" refers to nowadays, a software library. As far as I know, the hardware acceleration part of PhysX is now nothing but a dead gimmick. While Unity and Unreal both use PhysX, making it a very popular physics engine, neither of them support hardware acceleration of physics. I guess mostly because it would not work on most devices (only PC NVIDIA cards, not Android, etc) and might affect their performance negatively.

text:
Plus, it's doubtful that developers will in the end use it except for niche games. Practically speaking, if a developer team decides to include the RT system for lighting, they would need to create practically 2 games - one with the current system and one with the RT system. Because lighting with real time RT setup is completely different than without. The same goes for the reflection part. If one gamer can for example see an enemy in an reflection because they bought the better hardware but the other players who don't have the RTX can't see them, then it's a clear advantage. In other words, pay to win. 
So in the end, the developers would either make more work for themselves which will cost a lot more money or they will split the player-base in half just for making sure players can play their games with normal mode or hybrid mode. 
It will be much later down the line where the Hybrid mode is a lot more incorporated in every normal-Joe's computer, most probably when all three large consoles have it included as well, when more mainstream game dev companies will actually include this system.
